{{Pi box}}
'''William Jones''', [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] (1675{{spnd}}1 July 1749<ref>{{cite book |last1=Roberts |first1=Gareth Ffowc |title=Cyfri'n Cewri |date=2020 |publisher=University Press Wales |isbn=978-1786835949 |page=57 }}</ref>) was a Welsh mathematician best known for his use of the symbol {{pi}} (the [[Greek language|Greek]] letter ''[[Pi]]'') to represent [[Pi|the ratio of the circumference of a circle to its diameter]]. He was a close friend of Sir [[Isaac Newton]] and Sir [[Edmund Halley]]. In November 1711, Jones became a [[fellow of the Royal Society]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://makingscience.royalsociety.org/people/na7728/william-jones|title=William Jones 1675 - 1749|work=People|publisher=Royal Society|access-date=2025-03-29}}</ref> and later served as the [[Royal Society]]'s vice-president.<ref name=rothman/>

==Early life==
William Jones was born as the son of Siôn Siôr (John George Jones) and Elizabeth Rowland in the parish of [[Llanfihangel Tre'r Beirdd]], about {{convert|4|mi}} west of [[Benllech]] on the [[Isle of Anglesey]] in Wales. He attended a [[charity school]] at [[Llanfechell]], also on the Isle of Anglesey, where his mathematical talents were spotted by the local landowner [[Thomas Bulkeley, 7th Viscount Bulkeley|Lord Bulkeley]], who arranged for him to work in a merchant's counting-house in [[London]].<ref name="St Andrews"/> His main patrons were the Bulkeley family of north [[Wales]], and later the [[Thomas Parker, 1st Earl of Macclesfield|Earl of Macclesfield]].<ref>''[[:cy:Cyfri'n Cewri|Cyfri'n Cewri]]'' by [[Gareth Ffowc Roberts]]; [[University of Wales Press]] (2020); p. 14.</ref>

==Early mathematical career==
Jones initially served at sea, teaching mathematics on board Navy ships between 1695 and 1702, where he became very interested in navigation and published ''A New Compendium of the Whole Art of Navigation'' in 1702,<ref name="St Andrews">{{mactutor|id=Jones|title=William Jones}}</ref> dedicated to a benefactor [[John Harris (writer)|John Harris]].<ref>
{{cite book|author=William Jones|title=A New Compendium of the Whole Art of Navigation |year=1702|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Gm9bAAAAQAAJ|access-date=3 February 2011}}</ref> In this work he applied mathematics to navigation, studying methods of calculating position at sea. After his voyages were over he became a mathematics teacher in London, both in coffee houses and as a private tutor to [[George Parker, future president of the Royal Society, 2nd Earl of Macclesfield|George Parker]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Macclesfield Collection |url=https://cudl.lib.cam.ac.uk/collections/macclesfield/1 |website=Cambridge Digital Library |publisher=University of Cambridge |access-date=8 January 2024}}</ref> the son of the future Earl of Macclesfield, and also the future [[Philip Yorke, 1st Earl of Hardwicke|Baron Hardwicke]].<ref name="St Andrews"/>

==Later career==
[[File:Synopsis Palmariorum Matheseos pi.jpg|left|thumb|Jones' usage of π]]
Jones published ''Synopsis Palmariorum Matheseos'' in 1706, a work which was intended for beginners and which included theorems on [[differential calculus]] and [[infinite series]]. This used {{pi}} for the ratio of circumference to diameter, following earlier abbreviations for the Greek word ''periphery'' (περιφέρεια) by [[William Oughtred]] and others.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/stream/SynopsisPalmariorumMatheseosOrANewIntroductionToTheMathematics/Synopsis_Palmariorum_Matheseos#page/n261/mode/1up|title=Synopsis Palmariorum Matheseos : or, a New Introduction to the Mathematics|last=Jones|first=William|year=1706|pages=243, 263|language=en}}</ref><ref name=rothman>{{Cite web|url=https://www.historytoday.com/patricia-rothman/william-jones-and-his-circle-man-who-invented-pi|title=William Jones and his Circle: The Man who invented Pi|last=Rothman|first=Patricia|date=7 July 2009|website=History Today|access-date=6 October 2017}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/alexs-adventures-in-numberland/2015/mar/14/pi-day-2015-william-jones-the-welshman-who-invented-pi|title=Pi Day 2015: meet the man who invented π|last=Roberts|first=Gareth Ffowc|date=14 March 2015|work=The Guardian|access-date=6 October 2017|language=en-GB|issn=0261-3077}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/what-is-pi-and-how-did-it/|title=What is pi, and how did it originate?|last=Bogart|first=Steven|work=Scientific American|access-date=6 October 2017|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171006062336/https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/what-is-pi-and-how-did-it/|archive-date=6 October 2017|url-status=dead|df=dmy-all}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Archibald|first=R. C.|date=1921|title=Historical Notes on the Relation <math>e^{-(\pi/2)} = i^i</math>|jstor=2972388|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|volume=28|issue=3|pages=121|doi=10.2307/2972388|quote=It was probably suggested to Jones by Oughtred who employed the symbol in a different sense.}}</ref> His 1711 work ''Analysis per quantitatum series, fluxiones ac differentias'' introduced the dot notation for [[Derivative|differentiation]] in calculus.<ref>{{cite book|title=The life and mind Oriental Jones|author=Garland Hampton Cannon|year=1990|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=V7vgzG1BtYgC|access-date=3 February 2011}}</ref> 

He was noticed and befriended by two of Britain's foremost mathematicians – [[Edmund Halley]] and [[Sir Isaac Newton]] – and was elected a fellow of the Royal Society in 1711. He later became the editor and publisher of many of Newton's manuscripts and built up an extraordinary library that was one of the greatest collections of books on science and mathematics ever known, and only recently fully dispersed.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://theconversation.com/how-a-farm-boy-from-wales-gave-the-world-pi-55917|title= How a farm boy from Wales gave the world pi|date= 14 March 2016|publisher= The Conversation|access-date= 14 March 2017}}</ref> Jones' Last Will and Testament left his library, along with his gold watch, to [[George Parker, 2nd Earl of Macclesfield|Earl of Macclesfield]] in acknowledgement of his support.<ref>{{cite web |title=Last Will and Testament of William Jones (MS Add.9597/1/1) |url=https://cudl.lib.cam.ac.uk/view/MS-ADD-09597-00001-00001/1 |website=Cambridge Digital Library |publisher=University of Cambridge |access-date=8 January 2024}}</ref> 
 
==Personal life==
He married twice, firstly the widow of his counting-house employer, whose property he inherited on her death, and secondly, in 1731, Mary, the 22-year-old daughter of cabinet-maker George Nix, with whom he had two surviving children. His son, also named [[William Jones (philologist)|William Jones]] and born in 1746, was a renowned [[philologist]] who established links between Latin, Greek and Sanskrit, leading to the concept of the [[Indo-European language]] group.<ref name=Roberts2015>{{cite web|last1=Roberts|first1=Gareth Ffowc|title=Pi Day 2015: meet the man who invented π|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/alexs-adventures-in-numberland/2015/mar/14/pi-day-2015-william-jones-the-welshman-who-invented-pi|work=The Guardian|access-date=14 March 2015|date=14 March 2015}}</ref>
